sections.figure_alt: A magnitude sketch that falls, then falls more steeply.
sections.body_md:
Negative feedback oscillates when the loop returns a signal upside down and at least as large as the signal that was sent. Upside down is phase \(-180^\circ\). As large as the injected signal is magnitude \(1\). Two margins measure the distance to that point, in rad/s on the frequency axis.

The phase margin is \(180^\circ\) plus the phase at the gain crossover, the frequency where \(|L|=1\). The gain margin is \(1/|L|\) at the phase crossover, the frequency where the phase is \(-180^\circ\). If the phase never reaches \(-180^\circ\), there is no phase crossover and the gain margin is infinite.

A single pole in the open left half-plane contributes a phase between \(0^\circ\) and \(-90^\circ\). It cannot reach \(-180^\circ\), so a one-pole loop under negative feedback does not meet the oscillation condition. A second pole can supply the rest of the lag. Where to put that pole is a later skill.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ \mathrm{PM} = 180^\circ + \angle L(j\omega_c), \quad |L(j\omega_c)| = 1. \]
\[ \mathrm{GM} = \frac{1}{|L(j\omega_{180})|}, \quad \angle L(j\omega_{180}) = -180^\circ. \]
In decibels the gain margin is \(20\log_{10}(\mathrm{GM})\). Both frequencies are in rad/s when the loop gain is written in \(s\). A positive phase margin and a gain margin above \(1\) mean this particular pair of crossings is on the stable side of the oscillation condition.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(L(s) = 6/(s+3)\). The magnitude is \(1\) when \(\sqrt{\omega^2+9} = 6\), so \(\omega = \sqrt{27}\) rad/s. The phase there is \(-\arctan(\sqrt{3}) = -60^\circ\). The phase margin is \(120^\circ\). The phase of this one pole never reaches \(-180^\circ\), so the gain margin is infinite. A second pole would have to be added before a phase crossover could exist.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Reporting the phase at gain crossover as the phase margin. The margin is \(180^\circ\) plus that phase.
- Reporting \(|L|\) at phase crossover as the gain margin. The margin is the reciprocal.
- Reading the phase margin at the phase crossover, or the gain margin at the magnitude crossover.
- Expecting one left-half-plane pole to reach \(-180^\circ\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A later skill chooses how large a phase margin to ask for, and turns a delay into a phase budget at the crossover. Another asks how close the frequency-response curve stays to the point \(-1\). An amplifier loop uses a second pole, placed relative to the crossover, before it can spend the gain margin this one-pole picture leaves infinite.
